question: What images does the prophet use to describe the coming of the LORD, and what two cities does he point to as the center of “Jacob's transgression”?
The noun פֶּשַׁע (pesha‘, “transgression, rebellion”) appears at the beginning and at the end of the chapter: what idea of sin does this word carry, and to whom is it attributed?
Why does the prophet, after announcing judgment, begin to lament and to go about “barefoot and naked,” and what does this reveal about him?
Micah weeps for the same people he denounces: how do you react when you see the wrongdoing of people or groups you belong to?
At what time of day do the unjust plan and at what time do they carry out their plans, and what do they covet and seize?
What kind of prophet do the people want to hear, according to verses 6 and 11, and why does Micah's word disturb them?
The verb פָּרַץ (parats, “break through”) describes the one who goes before the people: what scene of liberation do verses 12 and 13 draw after so much denunciation?
Plans made “on their beds” turn into action in the morning: what intentions fill your nights, and what do they produce in your days?
What strong image does the prophet use to describe the way the leaders treat the people?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice”) appears in verses 1, 8 and 9: what does it mean in Micah's mouth, and who should practice it?
Leaders, priests and prophets act for money and still say “is not the LORD among us?”: what false security does the text denounce?
Micah contrasts paid prophets with someone “filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD”: what can influence what you say or keep silent about?
What do the nations come to seek on the mountain of the LORD, and what happens to swords and spears?
The same announcement of the mountain of the house of the LORD appears in Isaiah 2: why does this vision of peace come right after the destruction announced in 3:12?
The verb צָלַע (tsala‘, “limp”) describes those God will gather: what does it mean for God to form a strong people from “the lame”?
The image of each one under his own vine, without fear, describes a concrete peace: what does it inspire for life in your neighborhood or city?
What does verse 2 say about Bethlehem Ephrathah and about the one who will come forth from it?
The verb רָעָה (ra‘ah, “shepherd, rule”) links governing to the work of a shepherd: what kind of leadership does this image suggest?
Matthew 2:6 quotes this prophecy about Bethlehem: how do Jewish and Christian readings understand this ruler, and what do both highlight?
God says He will destroy the horses, chariots, strongholds and idols of His own people: why take away precisely these things?
God chooses Bethlehem, “small among the clans of Judah”: in what area of your life do you feel too small to be used?
What acts of God in Israel's history does the LORD remind the people of during His “lawsuit”?
The word רִיב (riv, “dispute, lawsuit”) sets up a courtroom scene: who are the witnesses, who accuses and who is accused?
Why does verse 8 answer the ever larger offerings of verses 6 and 7 with something so simple?
To act justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God: which of these three things is hardest for you today?
What practices of trade and of violence does the text denounce, and what kind of frustration is announced as a consequence?
How does the prophet describe the lack of faithful people, from the princes to within one's own household?
What change of tone happens from verse 7 on, and how does the prophet unite confession of sin and hope?
The book ends with חֶסֶד (chesed, “loving devotion, loyal love”): how do verses 18 to 20 join this word to the promise made to Abraham and Jacob?
“You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea”: what guilt do you still carry that you need to hand over this way?
